source.title: A Multi-Power Law for Loss Curve Prediction Across Learning Rate Schedules
source.authors: Kai-Rong Luo; Hao-Dong Wen; Sheng-Ding Hu; Zhenbo Sun; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun; Kaifeng Lyu; Wen-Guang Chen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates loss-curve prediction and power-law-based baselines with its own experiments, but its schedule-aware multi-power-law method differs from the original scaling-law methods.
record.gate_note: The study tests schedule-aware loss prediction and compares against a Chinchilla-style data-scaling law. It does not sweep parameter count or compute to test their scaling laws, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Downstream task scores compare schedules rather than testing whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own pretraining experiments on Llama-2 models from 25M to 400M, plus a 1B run, and argues that a plain power law in steps does not describe loss under decaying schedules. It shows that a Chinchilla-style data law fitted on final cosine losses is biased at intermediate steps and extrapolates worse. It restates the law as a power law in cumulative learning-rate sum plus a decay-induced correction. These results bear on V1 (token dimension only), V2 (short-range horizon extrapolation) and V7 (dependence on training schedule and fitting choices). It does not sweep parameters or compute, find a compute-optimal split, vary shape at fixed size, or test other modalities.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MPL predicts whole loss curves across unseen LR schedules and up to about 3x longer horizons, fitted on two or three runs. They report it as more sample-efficient than Chinchilla-style data laws and more accurate than the Momentum Law. They say it is accurate enough to derive schedules that beat cosine and tuned WSD. They acknowledge slight deviations for long horizons and high peak LRs, attributed to simplifying assumptions, and flag fitting robustness as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a schedule-aware multi-power law based on cumulative learning-rate sums and a loss-reduction correction, and fits whole loss curves. It is not a reproduction of the original parameter/token/compute scaling-law procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported accuracy degrades at higher peak learning rates; MPL coefficients vary with batch size. The authors also report fitting sensitivity to parameter initialization and optimization method, and slight deviations for long horizons.

fits_no_version.finding: A single power law in cumulative learning-rate sum fits constant-LR loss curves across peak LRs from 3e-4 to 3.6e-3 (R² 0.9976).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For constant-LR pretraining, loss is approximately a power law in cumulative LR sum, unifying runs with different peak LRs.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1B, the MPL-optimised schedule, which reaches lower loss than cosine, also scores higher on 5 of 6 downstream tasks (average +1.03, Table 2). This compares schedules, not a scale trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower pretraining loss from schedule changes at fixed size translates into downstream gains.

record.problems: The core prediction experiments use small model sizes up to 400M, with a separate 1B experiment, and test horizons up to about three times the training-set length rather than orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The paper reports slight prediction deviations for long-horizon and high-peak-learning-rate cases. It also notes that the fitting procedure can be sensitive to initialization and that Adam lacks theoretical convergence guarantees. A standard deviation across seeds is reported for a 25M experiment, but broad uncertainty estimates for the prediction metrics are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for schedule-optimization loss comparisons or downstream benchmark scores: those evaluate schedules, not the claim versions' scaling or predictability measures. Detailed figure-only curve values and individual schedule curves were not extracted where the text provides no separate numerical result. The paper's other model-architecture and random-seed descriptions were omitted unless they reported a separate result relevant to a tested version.

untested.parts: Power laws in parameter count or compute. Several orders of magnitude in tokens: only within-run curves up to 72000 steps are tested.
Extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger, and extrapolation across model sizes. Tested range is about 1.8–5x in training horizon at fixed model size.
Entire version: no fixed-compute sweep over parameters and tokens.
Entire version: no depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Entire version: no other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Entire version: downstream scores compare two schedules on one 1B model, not predictability from scale or loss.
Parameter-counting conventions and disagreement in compute-optimal splits across published laws.

missing.what: One-Power Law (LR-sum power law, no decay term) fit across schedules: R² 0.8309, MAE 0.0378, versus MPL R² 0.9975, 25M models
Cosine-fitted Chinchilla data law fails to fit the intermediate-step loss curve of open-source 7B OLMo trained with a linear schedule (figure only)
Fitted LR-sum exponent α differs by model size: 0.53 (25M), 0.46 (100M), 0.42 (400M)
1B model: MPL fitted on 24000-step curves predicts 72000-step constant and cosine curves (figure only, no numbers)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 label cited r02, which was not linked to V1; r01 is not a V1 test of power-law form. I re-linked r09 to V1, because constant LR with fixed batch makes LR sum proportional to tokens. Own-method (r02–r05) and baseline (r06–r08) rows are method comparisons: r02–r05 are kept for V2 with that caveat, and r06–r08 are set to none. Robustness rows r11–r14 do not measure a claim version. The original Kaplan and Hoffmann laws are not directly reproduced. The 'Chinchilla Data Scaling Law' here is a simplified, model-size-free version.

versions.untested_parts: No parameter-count or compute scaling sweep; the reported data-scaling comparison is schedule- and model-specific.
Prediction is tested mainly across schedule shapes and up to about three times the training-set horizon, not on runs orders of magnitude larger or on larger parameter counts.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameters and tokens.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling-law test.
Downstream task scores are compared across learning-rate schedules, not tested for predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study does not test disagreement in parameter-count or compute-optimal allocation exponents across published laws. It tests schedule-, learning-rate-, batch-size-, and fitting-related sensitivity.

rows.subject: 400M Llama-2 model
rows.operation_detail: Fit a Chinchilla Data Scaling Law to cosine-schedule final losses and predict a target cosine-schedule loss.
rows.note: The study reports this error for the Chinchilla Data Scaling Law; its MPL comparison has error 0.007 (r02).
rows.check: Not a V1 test: it measures extrapolation error of a data power law, not whether loss follows a power law. The Chinchilla Data Scaling Law fitted on final cosine losses up to 72000 steps predicts the 128000-step cosine loss (about 1.8x) with error 0.024, versus 0.007 for MPL. This bears on V7 because the fitting choice (final losses only, no schedule term) changes accuracy. Baseline should read 'MPL error 0.007 (r02)'.

source_check.correct: V2: cannot_determine; the comparison extrapolates from at most 72000 to 128000 steps and does not establish failure of orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The comparison with r02 bears on V7.

source_check.problem: The reported error alone does not establish a partial V2 effect.

rows.subject: 25M, 100M, and 400M Llama-2 models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law of cumulative learning-rate sum to constant-learning-rate loss curves.
rows.note: This is a power law in cumulative learning-rate sum, not a test of the parameters, tokens, or compute variables named by V1.
rows.check: Should be linked to V1. Under a constant learning rate and fixed batch size, cumulative LR sum is proportional to steps and tokens, so this is a power law of held-out loss in tokens: average R² 0.9947 over 25M, 100M and 400M models up to 72000 steps. The fit is to within-run loss curves, not separate runs, and covers well under several orders of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Constant-LR runs, 25M–400M Llama-2, up to 72000 steps
relationships.reason: Within-run validation loss follows a power law in LR sum, which is proportional to tokens at constant LR, with average R² 0.9947 (r09).
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss followed a power law in cumulative learning rate, proportional to tokens, with average R² of 0.9947.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Constant-LR runs, 25M–400M Llama-2, up to 72000 steps
source_check.reason: r09 confirms the fitted power-law form with average R² 0.9947. At fixed LR and batch size, cumulative LR is proportional to post-warmup tokens, with a fixed warmup offset. Support is confined to the tested range.

relationships.condition: Decaying LR schedules (cosine, WSD, step decay), 25M models
relationships.reason: Based on text not in rows: with no decay term the LR-sum power law fits poorly across schedules (Table 3 OPL R² 0.8309 vs MPL 0.9975). Applying the cosine-fitted step power law to intermediate steps is biased (Fig. 8b). So the token power law holds only within a fixed schedule family.
relationships.display_finding: Adding decay improved R² from 0.8309 to 0.9975 across schedules, while a cosine-fitted step law gave biased intermediate-step predictions.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Decaying LR schedules (cosine, WSD, step decay), 25M models
source_check.reason: Appendix A and Table 3 show that the LR-sum-only law requires schedule-dependent correction: R² 0.8309 versus 0.9975. The additional Figure 8(b) evidence concerns 7B OLMo with linear decay, outside this condition group; the study does not prove that all valid token laws are restricted to one schedule family.

relationships.condition: Horizon extrapolation of about 3–5x at fixed model size (25M–400M)
relationships.reason: A power-law-form law fitted on 24000-step runs predicts a 128000-step loss with error 0.007 (r02). Table 1 aggregates, which include 72000-step runs, give R² 0.997–0.998 (r03–r05).
relationships.display_finding: A fit from 24000 steps predicted loss at 128000 steps with error 0.007; aggregate evaluations including 72000-step runs achieved R² 0.997–0.998.

relationships.condition: Training schedule and fitting method, 25M–400M Llama-2
relationships.reason: The data law's accuracy depends on fitting final losses only from one schedule family (r01: 0.024 vs 0.007). Text not in rows adds three points. A single power law misfits decaying-schedule curves (Table 3 OPL R² 0.8309). MPL coefficients depend on batch size. The L-BFGS fit is initialization-sensitive.
relationships.display_finding: Prediction errors are 0.024 versus 0.007 depending on the restriction to final losses from one schedule family; a single power law yields R²=0.8309 on decaying schedules, multi-power-law coefficients depend on batch size, and L-BFGS fitting is sensitive to initialization.
